Check loaded rules

Codex AGENTS.md: Which Instructions Load?

Put shared rules in the repository root’s AGENTS.md. For rules specific to a subdirectory, add a file there and launch Codex from that directory or below it. Codex reads global rules first, then walks from the repository root to its starting directory. If a rule is missing, check the launch directory and look for a same-directory AGENTS.override.md.

  1. See the loading order
  2. Find the missing rule
  3. Check override files
  4. Check custom names and size
  5. Inspect the local prompt

Where Codex looks for AGENTS.md

  1. Global. Check ${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex} for shared instructions. AGENTS.override.md takes precedence there.
  2. Repository. Read one selected document per directory from the Git root down to the starting directory. An override takes precedence over AGENTS.md in its own directory. The nearest selected document appears last.
  3. Outside a project. When Codex cannot identify a project root, it checks only the current directory for project instructions.

For a task scoped to services/billing, open a fresh session at that path. A session started at the repository root can edit billing files without having loaded billing’s rules during startup. It also skips sibling folders such as services/search.

git rev-parse --show-toplevel
codex --cd services/billing

Use the root file for shared commands and rules. Use the billing file for a precise local rule such as Run make test-billing after changing this service. After editing the files, check from a fresh launch.

Which rule is missing?

Check for an empty AGENTS.override.md

If two instruction files sit in the same directory, first check the override’s content. In a local Codex CLI 0.172.0 test, a zero-byte or whitespace-only AGENTS.override.md still suppressed the same-directory AGENTS.md. The parent rules stayed in the prompt. Removing the override restored the base file in the next run.

Before changing a shared override, check whether it was intentional. If you maintain it and want the base rules back, rename it outside the configured instruction names or remove it after reviewing the change. Restart and verify that a distinctive line from the base file appears.

Check custom filenames and the byte limit

If the folder uses a different filename, put its exact name in the top-level Codex configuration. The file is only considered after AGENTS.override.md and AGENTS.md in that directory.

project_doc_fallback_filenames = ["TEAM_GUIDE.md"]

For rules missing late in a long chain, check project_doc_max_bytes. OpenAI documents a default of 32 KiB for project instructions. Shorten the earlier files or adjust that limit and check again from a fresh invocation. OpenAI’s discovery reference explains both settings.

Verify what actually reached the local prompt

In Codex CLI 0.172.0, debug prompt-input printed the assembled input without a model request in our network-blocked test. From the directory you want to check, search for a short, distinctive phrase already in the expected instruction file.

codex debug prompt-input "Check project instructions" |
  grep -Fq 'Run make test-billing after changing this service.'

Exit status 0 means the phrase appeared. If it is absent, confirm the debug command itself ran successfully, then compare a fresh run from the Git root and the target directory. Keep full prompt dumps local because they may include real project instructions and paths. A phrase in the input confirms loading. Model adherence requires a separate check.

Download the eight synthetic checks. They record the marker order on macOS in Codex CLI 0.172.0, including global overrides, sibling exclusion, fallback names and both forms of empty project override.
